title: Middlesboro, a town built inside a meteor crater
summary: About 300 million years ago an impact carved a basin west of Cumberland Gap. In 1889 Middlesboro was built inside it, unaware it sat in a crater.
bodyMarkdown:
Middlesboro sits in a bowl. Stand at the Pinnacle Overlook in [Cumberland Gap](https://grokipedia.com/page/Cumberland_Gap) and the whole town lies spread across a round, nearly flat basin about three miles wide, walled by Pine Mountain on the northwest and the Cumberland Mountains on the southeast. For most of the town’s life people took it for an ordinary mountain valley. It is the scar of a collision from space.

## The impact

Geologists estimate that a stony body about half a kilometer across struck here at roughly 20 kilometers a second, sometime in the late Pennsylvanian or early Permian period, [roughly 300 million years ago](https://grokipedia.com/page/Middlesboro_crater). The blow released on the order of 40 exajoules, about 10 gigatons of TNT, shattered the coal-bearing sandstones and shales of the [Pennsylvanian](https://grokipedia.com/page/Pennsylvanian_%28geology%29) Breathitt Group, and pushed up a central peak of broken rock ringed by faults. The finished crater was about 5.5 to 6 kilometers across.

The Appalachians were already standing when the rock fell, so it did not hit a smooth plain. The strike reactivated old thrust faults, including the Pine Mountain thrust, and bent the crater out of round. Since then erosion has stripped away about 1.5 kilometers of rock, nearly a mile, from above, leaving the deep roots of the structure at the surface.

## How the crater was recognized

To surveyors the basin was just an odd circle in a country of long, straight ridges. U.S. Geological Survey mappers flagged it as a possible impact scar in the early 1960s, and in 1966 [shatter cones](https://grokipedia.com/page/Shatter_cone), the striated, cone-shaped fractures that form only under shock pressure, were found in sandstone from the central uplift. Later work found shocked quartz with microscopic planar deformation features. Those clues make Middlesboro a confirmed impact crater, not a suspected one like [Jeptha Knob](/stories/jeptha-knob-shelby-countys-buried-crater/) in Shelby County.

## A town in the bowl

The people who built [Middlesboro](https://grokipedia.com/page/Middlesboro,_Kentucky) had no idea. In 1886 the Scottish-born promoter Alexander A. Arthur, backed by British investors in the American Association, Ltd., set out to build an iron and steel city in the flat ground just west of the Gap. English developers who came with the venture [laid out a golf course in 1889](https://history.ky.gov/markers/middlesboro-golf-club), one of the oldest in the country. The [Louisville and Nashville Railroad](https://grokipedia.com/page/Louisville_and_Nashville_Railroad) arrived that same year, and the city, [built in 1889](https://history.ky.gov/markers/middlesboro-meteorite-crater-impact-site) inside the basin, boomed with hotels, furnaces and a 100-foot-wide main avenue.

The boom broke in the 1890s, when the Baring Brothers bank failed, the Panic of 1893 hit, and the local iron ore proved too poor to carry a steel industry. Coal carried the town instead. The seams that the impact had broken and folded made Middlesboro what is believed to be the only place in the world where coal has been mined inside an impact crater.

## Kentucky today

The Kentucky Society of Professional Geologists named the crater a Distinguished Geological Site, and a state historical marker on 12th Street explains it. From the Pinnacle Overlook the ring is plain to see.

The map pin marks that marker. The years on this story are the town’s founding in the basin; the crater itself is roughly 300 million years old.
Source: [Grokipedia: Middlesboro crater](https://grokipedia.com/page/Middlesboro_crater)
